s: Which of the following pairs of removal motions against Lok Sabha Speakers is correctly matched?
x: Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed. The motion concerning Om Birla was listed for debate in 2026, not 1987.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: First Speaker of the Lok Sabha – Meira Kumar
x: G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker (1952–56); Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker and Sumitra Mahajan the second.

s: Who was the first Chairman of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council?
x: Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Council Chairman; Kalluri Subbarao was Deputy Speaker and Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao Speaker of the first Assembly.

s: Who was the first elected Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925)?
x: Vithalbhai Patel was the first elected Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925–30).

s: Who is known as the 'Father of the Lok Sabha'?
x: G.V. Mavalankar, the first Lok Sabha Speaker (1952–56), is called the Father of the Lok Sabha.

s: Who was the second woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: Sumitra Mahajan (16th Lok Sabha, 2014–19) was the second woman Speaker after Meira Kumar.

s: Which of the following pairs (Speaker – year of failed removal motion) is correctly matched?
x: Failed removal motions were against Mavalankar (1954), Hukum Singh (1966) and Balram Jakhar (1987); the Om Birla motion was rejected in March 2026.

s: Which office did M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar hold in the first Lok Sabha before he became Speaker in 1956?
o: Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee
x: M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar was the first Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and became Speaker after Mavalankar's death in 1956.

s: Who among the following Speakers of the Lok Sabha later became President of India?
x: N. Sanjiva Reddy, Speaker in 1967-69, is the only President who was earlier Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

s: Who was the Speaker of the first Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh (1956)?
x: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the first Speaker; Kalluri Subbarao was Deputy Speaker and Madapati Hanumantha Rao the first Council Chairman.

s: Who was the first Deputy Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly (1956)?
x: In the first AP Legislature (1956) Kalluri Subbarao was Deputy Speaker; Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was Speaker.

s: What is the voting right of the Speaker in normal sittings of the Lok Sabha?
o: does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in a tie
votes in the first instance and also has a casting vote
votes in the first instance like any member
x: Under Article 100 the Speaker does not vote in the first instance but gives a casting vote when votes are tied.

s: If both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are absent from a joint sitting of Parliament, who presides over it?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
x: The Speaker presides over a joint sitting (Art. 118(4)), then the Deputy Speaker, then the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the powers of the Speaker?
o: The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition, subject to the party-strength requirement.
The Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are beyond judicial review.
The Speaker appoints chairmen of parliamentary committees.
Rulings of the Speaker are protected by Article 122.
x: The Speaker decides Tenth Schedule cases, but those decisions remain subject to judicial review.

s: According to the Speaker's direction, what minimum strength must a party have for its leader to be recognised as Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha?
x: Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction. The office has statutory status since the 1977 Act.

s: Under which Article is the Speaker's certificate endorsed on a Money Bill given?
x: Under Article 110(4) the Speaker certifies a Money Bill, and the certificate is final; the Rajya Sabha cannot overrule it.

s: Which Article gives the Speaker the power to decide whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
x: Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's decision on a Money Bill final; the certificate is endorsed under 110(4).

s: In which year did an Act give statutory status to the post of Leader of the Opposition?
x: The Speaker recognises the LoP if the party has one-tenth of the House; the office became statutory under the 1977 Act.

s: Under which Article does the Speaker preside over a joint sitting of the two Houses?
x: The President summons a joint sitting under Article 108, and the Speaker presides under Article 118(4).

s: Who nominates the Panel of Chairpersons of the Lok Sabha?
x: The Speaker nominates up to ten members to the panel; one presides when both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Panel of Chairpersons of the Lok Sabha:
1. Its members are nominated by the Speaker.
2. A member of the Panel presides when the office of the Speaker is vacant.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Speaker nominates up to ten members; one presides when both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent, but not when the Speaker's office is vacant.

s: Up to how many members can the Speaker nominate to the Panel of Chairpersons of the Lok Sabha?
x: The Speaker nominates a Panel of up to ten Chairpersons from among the members.

s: What is the minimum advance notice required for a resolution to remove the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: Under Article 94 removal needs a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice; the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker.

s: Removal of which of the following requires NO advance notice?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: The President removes a Governor at pleasure without notice; the other three removals need 14 days' notice.

s: To whom does the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha address his resignation?
x: The Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker, and the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker, not to the President.

s: Which oath does the Speaker of the Lok Sabha take on assuming office?
o: only the oath as a Member of Parliament
a separate oath administered by the President
a separate oath administered by the Chief Justice of India
a separate oath administered by the Pro-Tem Speaker
x: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker take only the oath as MPs; there is no separate oath as presiding officer.

s: On which Fund are the salary and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha charged?
x: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 97.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
1. The Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. The Speaker takes a separate oath of office as Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund (Art 97), but there is no separate oath for the Speaker, only the oath as an MP.

s: Under which Article is the Speaker removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha?
x: Article 94(c) requires an effective majority, after 14 days' notice; a simple majority is not enough.

s: Who can be chosen Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: Any citizen, if elected to the House within six months
A member of either House of Parliament
Only an elected member of the Lok Sabha
A Rajya Sabha member nominated by the President
x: The Speaker must already be an elected Lok Sabha member; the six-month relaxation applies only to Ministers.

s: What may the Speaker of the Lok Sabha do while a resolution for his removal is under consideration?
o: Exercise a casting vote in a tie
x: Under Article 96 the Speaker cannot preside during his removal resolution but may speak and vote in the first instance, though not cast a vote in a tie.

s: Which Article provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: Article 93 provides that the House of the People shall choose two members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker.

s: The constitutional provisions governing the Speaker of the Lok Sabha are contained in which one of the following groups of Articles?
x: The Speaker is covered by Articles 93–96 (election, vacation, removal), 100 (casting vote), 110 (Money Bill certificate) and 118 (joint sitting rules).

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about presiding officers when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?
o: The Speaker vacates office immediately on dissolution.
The Speaker continues until just before the new Lok Sabha first meets.
The Deputy Speaker vacates office at once.
A State Speaker follows the same rule under Article 179.
x: The Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution; he continues until just before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha.

s: Under Article 179, to whom does the rule that the Speaker continues after dissolution apply?
o: The Speaker of a State Assembly
The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of a Legislative Council
x: Article 179 lays down the same rule for the State Speaker, who also continues till just before the new Assembly first meets.

s: What is the position of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha during consideration of a resolution for his own removal?
o: May vote in the first instance
x: The Chairman cannot preside or vote during his own removal resolution but may speak; the Speaker, by contrast, can vote in the first instance.

s: Which presiding officer of the Lok Sabha does NOT vacate office when the House is dissolved?
x: Only the Speaker stays in office after dissolution, till just before the new House first meets; the Deputy Speaker vacates at once.

s: Which Article provides that the Speaker shall not preside while a resolution for his removal is under consideration?
x: Article 96 bars the Speaker (or Deputy Speaker) from presiding during his own removal resolution; he may speak and vote in the first instance.

s: Who fixes the date of election of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: The President fixes the Speaker's election date and the Speaker fixes the Deputy Speaker's.

s: Which Article provides for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly?
x: Article 178 provides for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of a State Assembly, as Article 93 does for the Lok Sabha.

s: Which of the following statements regarding removal of the Deputy Speaker is incorrect?
o: The Deputy Speaker may be removed by the Lok Sabha.
Removal requires a two-thirds special majority.
Fourteen days' notice is required for the removal resolution.
x: Option B is incorrect: removing the Deputy Speaker needs an effective majority (a majority of all the then members), not two-thirds, after 14 days' notice.

s: What is the quorum of the Lok Sabha?
x: The quorum of the Lok Sabha is one-tenth of its total membership. One-fifth and one-third are distractors.

s: Which provision empowers the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha?
x: Article 85(2)(b) covers dissolution and 85(2)(a) prorogation; Article 123 is about ordinances.

s: What is the period between prorogation of Parliament and the commencement of its next session called?
x: The period from prorogation to the next session is called a recess. It is different from adjournment, which interrupts a sitting within a session.

s: What is ordinarily the quorum in either House of Parliament?
o: One-half of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-tenth of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-fourth of the elected membership, excluding nominated members
One-twentieth of the total membership, excluding the presiding officer
x: Under Article 100(3), the quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.

s: How is the six-month maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament counted?
o: the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next
the first sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next
the date of prorogation to the date of the next summons
the date of summons to the date of prorogation
x: The rule runs from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next; the Budget, Monsoon and Winter names are only conventions.

s: Which of the following is correct about the summoning of Parliament?
o: The President may summon the two Houses separately.
The Vice-President summons the Rajya Sabha.
Both Houses must always be summoned together.
x: The President need not summon both Houses together, but each must meet within six months of its last sitting.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Constitution mandates that Parliament must meet at least twice a year.
The maximum gap between two consecutive sessions cannot exceed six months.
The three-session pattern of Budget, Monsoon and Winter is a parliamentary convention.
The Constitution specifies a fixed number of parliamentary sessions every year.
x: Option D is incorrect: the Constitution sets no fixed number of sessions. It only sets a gap of at most six months (so at least two sessions a year); the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention.

s: Which Article fixes the quorum of a House of Parliament?
x: Article 100(3) fixes the quorum at one-tenth of total members, including the presiding officer.

s: Which session of Parliament is usually the longest?
x: The Budget Session (February–May) is the longest; the three sessions are a convention, not in the Constitution.

s: Which Article lays down the six-month rule for sessions of State Legislatures?
x: Article 174 applies the same six-month maximum gap to State Legislatures.

s: On what are the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions of Parliament based?
x: The three-session pattern is a convention, and the Constitution prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.

s: On average, about how many sittings did State Legislative Assemblies hold in 2025?
x: State Assemblies averaged only about 24 sittings in 2025.

s: Which of the following does NOT lapse on the prorogation of Parliament?
x: Bills do not lapse on prorogation, although pending notices generally lapse except notices to introduce bills.

s:
Assertion (A): Prorogation ends the very life of the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): Adjournment suspends the work in a sitting for a specified time.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Prorogation only ends a session; it is dissolution that ends the Lok Sabha itself. R correctly describes adjournment.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Adjournment – Presiding Officer, suspending a sitting for a specified time
Adjournment sine die – Presiding Officer, without naming a day of reassembly
x: The President prorogues under Article 85(2)(a); Article 85(2)(b) is dissolution.

s: Under which Article is the lapse of pending bills on dissolution of the Lok Sabha governed?
x: Dissolution ends the Lok Sabha and its pending business lapses, subject to Article 107; the Rajya Sabha is permanent.

s: Under which Article does the President prorogue the Lok Sabha?
x: Article 85(2)(a) empowers the President to prorogue; 85(2)(b) is dissolution.

s: On whose advice does the President prorogue the Houses of Parliament?
x: Prorogation is done by the President on the Council of Ministers' advice (the Governor in States); it ends the session, not the House.

s: Who orders an adjournment sine die of the Lok Sabha?
x: Adjournment and adjournment sine die are done by the presiding officer; prorogation and dissolution by the President.

s: What happens to pending bills on adjournment sine die of a House?
o: They go to a joint sitting
They are sent to the President
x: Adjournment sine die precedes prorogation and pending bills continue (APPSC 2025); bills lapse only on dissolution.

s: Under which Article may the President send messages to either House of Parliament regarding a pending Bill?
x: Article 86 lets the President address either or both Houses, require members' attendance and send messages on pending Bills.

s: Under which Article does the President make a special address at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year?
x: Article 87 provides for this special address; it is not required after every prorogation.

s: Through which motion is the President's address outlining the policies of the Government debated in Parliament?
x: The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a Motion of Thanks in Parliament.

s: The President's special address under Article 87 is made at the first session of each year and at the first session after which event?
x: Article 87 requires a special address at the first session after each general election and of each year, not after every prorogation.

s: Under Article 86, what else may the President do besides addressing the Houses?
x: Article 86 lets the President address either or both Houses, require members' attendance and send messages on pending Bills.

s: What is the constitutional quorum for a House of Parliament?
x: Under Article 100, the quorum of either House is one-tenth of its total membership.

s:
Assertion (A): The gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months.
Reason (R): Article 85 implies that Parliament must have at least two sessions in a year.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true: Article 85 bars a gap of more than six months between sessions, and so Parliament must meet at least twice a year. R is a consequence of A, not its explanation.

s: To whom does the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha address his resignation?
x: The Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman and can be removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice.

s: Under which Article is a resolution to remove the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha provided?
x: Article 90(c) provides for removal of the Deputy Chairman by an effective majority of the Rajya Sabha after 14 days' notice.

s: How can the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha be removed from office?
o: By a two-thirds vote of the Rajya Sabha
x: The Vice-President is ex officio Chairman, so he leaves the Chair only on removal as Vice-President.

s: When the Vice-President acts as President, who performs the duties of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
Leader of the House in the Rajya Sabha
x: The Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties when the Vice-President acts as President.

s: What is the counterpart in the Rajya Sabha of the Lok Sabha's Panel of Chairpersons?
x: The Rajya Sabha has a Panel of Vice-Chairpersons nominated by the Chairman.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court in January 2026 uphold the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman's power under Article 91 to decide a judge-removal motion when the Chairman's office was vacant?
x: In the Justice Varma case (January 2026), the Supreme Court upheld the Deputy Chairman's power under Article 91 to decide a judge-removal motion while the Chairman's office was vacant.

s: As of 2026, who is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
x: C.P. Radhakrishnan, as Vice-President, is the ex officio Chairman; Harivansh was Deputy Chairman (term ended 9 April 2026) and S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman (1952-62).

s: Who was the first Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
x: S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman (1952–62); C.P. Radhakrishnan is the present Chairman.

s: Whose salary does the Vice-President draw when he acts as President?
x: While acting as President, the Vice-President draws the President's salary, and the Deputy Chairman does the Chairman's work under Article 91.

s: What voting right does the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha have?
o: An ordinary vote in all divisions
A vote only on Money Bills
x: The Vice-President, as ex officio Chairman, is not a member of the Rajya Sabha and has only a casting vote.

s: Who served as Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha until his term ended on 9 April 2026?
x: Harivansh Narayan Singh was Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; his term ended on 9 April 2026.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Office)
A. Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (2026)
B. Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (till April 2026)
C. First Speaker of the Lok Sabha
D. First woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha
List-II (Person)
1. G.V. Mavalankar
2. Meira Kumar
3. Harivansh
4. C.P. Radhakrishnan
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: C.P. Radhakrishnan is the present Chairman, Harivansh was Deputy Chairman, Mavalankar was the first LS Speaker and Meira Kumar the first woman Speaker.

s: Under whose control and guidance does the Lok Sabha Secretariat function directly?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: The Lok Sabha Secretariat works directly under the Speaker's control and guidance, not under the executive, which keeps the House independent.

s: Until Parliament makes a law regulating recruitment and service conditions of the secretarial staff of the Houses, with whom does the President consult before making rules?
o: Chief Justice of India and Attorney-General of India
Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and Secretary-General of the Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister and Union Home Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

s: Which Article provides separate secretarial staff for each House of Parliament?
x: Article 98 gives each House its own secretarial staff while permitting posts common to both Houses.

s: Who appoints the Secretary-General of a House of Parliament?
x: The Secretary-General is appointed by the presiding officer of the House, keeping the secretariat independent of the executive.

s: The Secretary-General of each House of Parliament holds a rank equal to that of which officer?
x: The Secretary-General, appointed by the presiding officer, holds the rank of the Cabinet Secretary.

s: Who raised the idea of a separate secretariat for the legislature in 1926?
x: Vithalbhai Patel, Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly, raised the separate secretariat idea in 1926.

s: Who is usually appointed Speaker Pro Tem of a newly elected Lok Sabha?
o: The senior-most member of the House
x: The Speaker Pro Tem is the senior-most member, sworn in by the President; the outgoing Speaker only stays in office until just before the new House first meets.

s: Who administers the oath to newly elected members of the Lok Sabha?
x: The Pro-Tem Speaker swears in the new MPs and conducts the election of the regular Speaker.

s: Under which Article does the President appoint the Pro-Tem Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1); only the regular Speaker is elected under Article 93.

s: Which of the following statements regarding the Pro-Tem Speaker is incorrect?
o: The Pro-Tem Speaker performs temporary functions until the regular Speaker is elected
The Pro-Tem Speaker is elected by the members of the newly elected Lok Sabha
The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most elected MP of the newly elected House
The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President
x: Option B is incorrect: the Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1), not elected by the House. The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most member and serves until the regular Speaker is elected.

s: On what does the practice of choosing the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker from the Opposition rest?
o: Rule 8(1) of the Lok Sabha Rules
x: The Deputy Speaker is elected by the House from its members; picking an Opposition member is only a convention, not a constitutional requirement.

s: What can the Deputy Speaker do while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration?
x: The Deputy Speaker cannot preside then but may speak, take part and vote in the first instance; no casting vote is allowed.

s: When does the tenure of the Pro-Tem Speaker end?
x: The Pro-Tem Speaker administers oath and holds the Speaker's election; his role ends once the regular Speaker is elected.

s: To whom is the list of senior members for appointing the Pro-Tem Speaker sent?
x: The President appoints the senior-most member as Pro-Tem Speaker; the list of senior members goes to the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs.

s: What is the status of a ruling given by the Deputy Speaker while in the Chair?
o: can be appealed to the Speaker
must be ratified by the Speaker
cannot be appealed to the Speaker
can be appealed to the President
x: While presiding, the Deputy Speaker has the Speaker's powers, and his rulings cannot be appealed to the Speaker.

s: Under Rule 8(1), who fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election, which is then notified by the Secretary-General?
x: The Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election and the Secretary-General notifies it to members.

s: Who communicates the date of election of the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha to all members?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha
x: The Speaker fixes the Deputy Speaker's election date under Rule 8(1), and the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha communicates it to all members.

s: Who appoints the Pro-Tem Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
x: The President appoints the Pro-Tem Speaker; adjourning sine die, Tenth Schedule decisions and fixing the Deputy Speaker's election date are the Speaker's.

s: What can the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha do when not in the Chair?
o: can only give a casting vote
can debate, move motions and vote in the first instance
x: Out of the Chair the Deputy Speaker is an ordinary member who can debate, move motions and vote in the first instance, unlike the Speaker.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: The Deputy Speaker is elected after the election of the Speaker.
The Deputy Speaker resigns by writing to the Speaker.
The Deputy Speaker is subordinate to the Speaker in exercising the office's functions.
The Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting when the Speaker is absent.
x: The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker while exercising the functions of the office.

s: Since when has the office of Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha been vacant?
x: The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019; the office was also reported vacant in eight State Assemblies.

s: What happens when the Deputy Speaker is appointed to a parliamentary committee?
o: Needs the Speaker's approval to attend
x: The Deputy Speaker automatically becomes the chairman of any committee he is appointed to.

s: In which State Assembly had the post of Deputy Speaker remained vacant for 21 years as of June 2026?
x: The Deputy Speaker post was vacant in 8 State Assemblies, and in Jharkhand for 21 years (June 2026).

s: By what majority must a resolution to remove the Lok Sabha Speaker under Article 94(c) be passed?
o: A majority of all the then members of the House
A simple majority of members present and voting
Two-thirds of members present and voting
x: Removal needs a majority of all the then members (an effective majority), after 14 days' notice; a simple majority is not enough.

s: During which time does asking and answering questions addressed to Ministers take place?
x: Question Hour is for questions to Ministers; Zero Hour is informal and needs no notice.

s: Which of the following parliamentary devices is informal and not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure?
x: Zero Hour, which follows Question Hour, is informal; Question Hour is formal and provided in the Rules.

s: What is the primary purpose of Question Hour in Parliament?
o: Discuss only matters of urgent public importance
Enforce accountability of the Council of Ministers
x: Question Hour and related hours exist to enforce executive accountability and control over the Council of Ministers.

s: Which of the following is correct about Zero Hour and the Calling Attention Motion?
o: Expressly provided for in the Constitution
Created by the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Borrowed from the British House of Commons
Indian innovations not mentioned in the Constitution
x: Both grew out of Indian parliamentary practice; neither is mentioned in the Constitution, and Zero Hour is not even in the Rules.

s: Since which year has Zero Hour, an informal Indian parliamentary innovation, been in use?
x: Zero Hour dates from 1962 and is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure; 1953 and 1954 are the short-duration discussion and calling attention.

s: To raise a matter during Zero Hour, a member:
o: intimates the Presiding Officer on the same day
gives the same notice as for an ordinary question
needs the consent of the Minister concerned
x: Zero Hour needs no ordinary-question notice; members intimate the Presiding Officer the same day, and it has no fixed duration in the Rules.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of matters raised during Zero Hour?
o: The Presiding Officer decides which members may be allowed to raise them
Members may raise them without the prior notice required for a question
Ministers are constitutionally bound to give an immediate reply
They concern urgent matters of public importance
x: Ministers are not bound to reply to matters raised during Zero Hour. The other features correctly describe the procedure.

s: In the Lok Sabha, what is the time immediately after Question Hour, when members raise urgent matters without prior notice, called?
x: Zero Hour begins immediately after Question Hour; members raise matters with only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer.

s: Which of the following statements regarding the post-2014 arrangement is incorrect?
o: In the Rajya Sabha, Question Hour is from 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM.
In the Lok Sabha, Question Hour is from 11:00 AM to 12:00 Noon.
In the Lok Sabha, Zero Hour is from 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM.
In the Rajya Sabha, Zero Hour is from 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM.
x: Option D is incorrect. Since 2014, the Rajya Sabha has Zero Hour from 11 AM to noon (not noon to 1 PM) and Question Hour from noon to 1 PM, the reverse of the Lok Sabha.

s: Since 2014, with what does the Rajya Sabha begin its day at 11 AM?
x: Since 2014 the Rajya Sabha has Zero Hour at 11 AM and Question Hour from noon to 1 PM; the Lok Sabha has Question Hour first.

s: Which of the following statements regarding Zero Hour is incorrect?
o: It has a maximum duration of one hour in the Lok Sabha.
It is used for raising urgent matters of public importance.
It is an informal parliamentary convention.
It is taken before Question Hour in the Lok Sabha.
x: Option D is incorrect: Zero Hour comes right after Question Hour (noon to 1 PM in the Lok Sabha), not before it. It is an informal convention lasting at most one hour.

s: At what time is Question Hour held in the Lok Sabha?
x: Question Hour is the first hour in the Lok Sabha, 11 AM to 12 Noon; Zero Hour follows from 12 Noon.

s: What is the minimum notice for an ordinary question in Parliament?
x: Ordinary questions need 15 clear days' notice; a short notice question is given with less than 10 days' notice.

s: What is the formal right of members to ask questions of the Executive called?
x: Interpellation is the formal right of asking questions of the Executive.

s: Through which body do directions given by the Chair during Zero Hour reach the ministry concerned?
x: The Chair's directions in Zero Hour go through the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs to the ministry concerned.

s: Which is regarded as the most powerful weapon for enforcing the accountability of the executive?
x: The no-confidence motion is the most powerful weapon of accountability and need not state reasons; Question Hour is the most effective day-to-day vigil.

s: From which Article does parliamentary control over the Council of Ministers mainly flow?
x: Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, the basis of parliamentary devices of control.

s: In which House can a Confidence Motion be moved?
o: a joint sitting of both Houses
x: Confidence motions are admissible only in the Lok Sabha.

s: What minimum support is needed for leave to move a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha?
x: It needs 50 members' support; the motion is not expressly in the Constitution but flows from Article 75(3) and lies only in the Lok Sabha.

s: Who moved the first no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers, against Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963?
x: The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by J.B. Kripalani.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A Censure Motion may be directed against a Minister, a group of Ministers or the whole Council.
A No-confidence Motion is directed against the entire Council of Ministers.
Passing a Censure Motion compels the Council of Ministers to resign.
Passing a No-confidence Motion requires the Council of Ministers to resign.
x: A passed Censure Motion does not compel resignation; a passed No-confidence Motion does.

s: What happens if a Confidence Motion moved by the Government is defeated in the Lok Sabha?
o: The Lok Sabha is automatically dissolved
The motion is referred to the Committee of Privileges
x: Defeat of a confidence motion shows the Government has lost the Lok Sabha's support, so it falls.

s: Who moves a Confidence Motion in the Lok Sabha?
x: The Government moves a confidence motion to prove its majority; a no-confidence motion is moved by the Opposition.

s: Which of the following pairs about a no-confidence motion is correctly matched?
o: House where moved – Lok Sabha only
Rule of the Lok Sabha – Rule 184
x: A no-confidence motion (Rule 198) is moved only in the Lok Sabha with 50 members' support and needs no reasons.

s: Which motion must state specific reasons for its adoption?
x: A censure motion must state reasons; a no-confidence motion needs 50 members' support but no reasons, and the government moves a confidence motion.

s: Who moved the no-confidence motion carried against the Prakasam ministry of Andhra State in November 1954?
x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion was carried by 69 votes to 68 in November 1954, and the Prakasam ministry fell.

s: Who decides whether a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha is admitted?
x: The Speaker has discretion to admit or reject a no-confidence motion; reasons need not be stated.

s: By what margin was the no-confidence motion against the Prakasam ministry of Andhra State (1954) carried?
x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion passed 69–68 and the Prakasam ministry fell by one vote after 13 months.

s: Against whom is a no-confidence motion directed?
x: A no-confidence motion is against the whole Council of Ministers; if passed, the whole CoM must resign.

s: To whom is notice of a no-confidence motion given in writing?
x: Written notice goes to the Secretary-General, and at least 50 members must support leave to move it.

s: What happens if a censure motion against a minister is passed?
x: A censure motion expresses disapproval of policy; unlike a no-confidence motion, it does not force resignation.

s: When was President's Rule imposed in Andhra State after the Prakasam ministry fell by one vote?
x: After Gouthu Latchanna's no-confidence motion passed 69-68, President's Rule ran from 16 November 1954 to 27 March 1955.

s: When a member who is speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair, what is the procedure known as?
x: Yielding the floor occurs when the member speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Simple closure — Only important clauses are debated
Closure by compartments — All pending clauses are voted on when time ends
Kangaroo closure — Only important clauses are debated and the others are taken as passed
Guillotine — Matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote
x: C is correct: under kangaroo closure only the important clauses are debated and the rest are taken as passed. A is wrong because simple closure means the matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote; B is wrong because putting all pending clauses to vote when time ends is the guillotine; D is wrong because it describes simple closure, not the guillotine.

s: What is the form of closure called in which all remaining clauses or demands are put to vote at once when the allotted time expires?
x: The guillotine is the form of closure applied when the allotted time runs out, putting all remaining clauses or demands to vote at once.

s: How is a point of order raised in the House dealt with?
o: Allows no debate and is ruled on by the presiding officer
Is followed by a full debate
Is referred to the Rules Committee
x: A point of order is raised when proceedings depart from the rules; there is no debate and the presiding officer rules on it.

s: Which closure is the one in which only important clauses are debated and the rest are taken as passed?
x: Kangaroo closure debates only the important clauses; the guillotine puts undiscussed clauses to vote when time ends.

s: Which of the following is considered the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive?
x: Question Hour is regarded as the most effective day-to-day check on the executive because Ministers must answer questions.

s: What are Question Hour, supplementary questions and adjournment motions together described as?
x: Together they let Parliament question the government, follow up and raise urgent matters, forming the 'accountability triangle'.

s: Besides Question Hour and motions, through which of the following do State Legislatures control the executive?
x: State Legislatures use the same parliamentary devices and also estimates and public accounts committees.

s: Which of the following is a tool of parliamentary control over the executive?
x: The half-an-hour discussion is a parliamentary device; judicial review is a function of the judiciary, not Parliament.

s: In which year was the Calling Attention device introduced?
x: Calling Attention dates from 1954; the short-duration discussion is from 1953 and Zero Hour is associated with 1962.

s: An Adjournment Motion can be admitted only when it concerns which of the following?
o: A demand for grant requiring reduction by one rupee
Any matter raised without prior notice
A matter of definite and urgent public importance
x: An Adjournment Motion sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.

s: Which one of the following motions is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from a Minister?
x: A Calling Attention Motion is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from the concerned Minister.

s: Historically, the operational scope of which parliamentary motion was restricted by Calling Attention notices?
x: Calling attention notices narrowed the scope of adjournment motions by offering a milder way to raise urgent matters. Question Hour and Zero Hour were not affected.

s: An Adjournment Motion is admissible only when which condition is satisfied?
o: Other tools, such as a Short Duration discussion, are too late
The matter concerns a question of privilege
A matter has already been fully debated in Question Hour
The scheduled daily agenda has been completed
x: An adjournment motion is admitted only when other routes, such as a short duration discussion, would come too late. Questions of privilege cannot be raised this way.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about an Adjournment Motion?
o: The debate on it lasts not less than two hours and thirty minutes.
It needs the support of 50 members for admission.
It can be moved in either House of Parliament.
It must relate to a single, definite matter of recent occurrence.
x: An Adjournment Motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A Calling Attention Motion does not disrupt the scheduled daily agenda.
An Adjournment Motion interrupts normal parliamentary business.
A Calling Attention Motion involves censure of the Government.
An Adjournment Motion involves an element of censure of the Government.
x: A Calling Attention Motion has no element of censure; it is the Adjournment Motion that implies censure.

s: What is the minimum duration of the debate on an admitted Adjournment Motion?
x: An adjournment motion suspends normal business, and its debate lasts at least 2 hours 30 minutes.

s: How many adjournment motions can be taken up in a single sitting?
x: Only one adjournment motion is allowed per sitting, on a definite matter of recent occurrence.

s: Which of the following is NOT a feature of an Adjournment Motion?
o: It is moved only in the Lok Sabha.
It can raise a question of privilege.
It needs the support of 50 members.
It involves an element of censure.
x: An adjournment motion cannot raise a question of privilege; it is a Lok Sabha device needing 50 members and carries censure.

s: Unlike an adjournment motion, a calling attention motion:
o: Can be moved only in the Lok Sabha
Sets aside the normal business of the House
x: A calling attention motion seeks a Minister's statement without censure and is allowed in either House with the presiding officer's permission.

s: At most how many starred questions are listed per day for oral answer?
x: Starred questions are limited to 20 a day for oral answer; unstarred questions have no such limit.

s: Which type of question deals with matters of urgent public importance?
x: Short notice questions concern urgent matters; starred and unstarred questions concern matters of general public importance.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Question to a private member — Blue paper
x: A question addressed to a private member is printed on yellow paper, not blue paper. Starred, unstarred and short-notice questions are associated with green, white and light pink paper respectively.

s: Which question gets a written answer, with no supplementary questions allowed?
x: Unstarred questions get written answers without supplementaries; starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries.

s: Supplementary questions are allowed on which of the following?
x: Starred and short notice questions get oral answers and allow supplementaries; unstarred questions get written answers without them.

s: Which parliamentary questions are marked with an asterisk?
x: Starred questions carry an asterisk; unstarred questions do not, and a short notice question is known by its shorter notice.

s: Which of the following is not one of the three primary categories of Parliamentary Questions?
x: The three kinds of parliamentary question are starred, unstarred and short notice. There is no 'adjournment question'; adjournment is a motion.

s: The daily listing of Short Notice Questions is at the discretion of whom?
o: The Leader of the House only
x: Short notice questions are listed each day at the discretion of the Speaker or Chairman, who decides whether the matter is urgent enough.

s: What is a White Paper?
o: A report of the Committee on Petitions
An official Government document explaining its policy on a subject
The record of Zero Hour proceedings
x: A White Paper is an official Government document explaining policy on a subject, often to gather views before a bill.

s: Which of the following pairs (question – colour of paper) is correctly matched?
o: Question to a private member – Blue
x: Short notice questions are on light pink paper; starred are green, unstarred white and questions to private members yellow.

s: A short-notice question differs from an ordinary question in that it may be admitted when notice is given how far in advance?
o: Only on the day of the sitting
At least 15 clear days in advance
x: A short-notice question is one for which notice is given less than 10 days in advance. Ordinary questions require at least 15 clear days' notice.

s: In which year was the short-duration discussion, an Indian parliamentary innovation, introduced?
x: The short-duration discussion dates from 1953; it is limited to two hours and involves no vote.

s:
Consider the following statements about Indian parliamentary innovations:
1. The short-duration discussion was introduced in 1953.
2. The calling attention motion was introduced in 1962.
3. Zero Hour is not mentioned in the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The short-duration discussion dates from 1953 and Zero Hour (1962) is not in the Constitution; calling attention came in 1954, not 1962.

s: Under which Rule is a short-duration discussion without voting held in the Lok Sabha?
x: Rule 193 is a discussion without voting, Rule 184 a discussion followed by voting, and Rule 377 is for matters not raisable under any other device.

s: What mainly governs the day-to-day proceedings of the Lok Sabha?
o: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha
x: The Constitution gives only the broad framework; devices such as the No-Confidence Motion and Rule 377 come from the Rules of Procedure.

s: Under which Rule is a matter that cannot be raised through questions, calling attention or other motions raised in the Lok Sabha?
x: Rule 377 covers such matters; it requires written notice and the Speaker's consent.

s: Under which Rules of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha respectively is a privilege motion raised?
x: A privilege motion is governed by Rule 222 of the Lok Sabha rules and Rule 187 of the Rajya Sabha rules. Rule 184 (LS) is a discussion followed by a vote, Rule 193 (LS) is a short-duration discussion without a vote, Rule 180A-E (RS) covers Special Mentions, and Rule 198 (LS) is the no-confidence motion.

s: Under which rule of the Lok Sabha is a discussion followed by a formal motion and voting held?
x: Rule 184 allows a discussion ending in a formal motion and vote, and defeat on it can threaten the ruling party.

s: On what kind of matter is a half-an-hour discussion held in Parliament?
o: A matter of urgent public importance requiring adjournment of the House
A matter already sufficiently debated but requiring factual elucidation
x: A half-an-hour discussion is held on a matter sufficiently debated that needs further factual elucidation; it involves no formal motion or vote.

s: What is the maximum duration of a short-duration discussion under Rule 193?
x: A Rule 193 discussion lasts at most 2 hours and has no vote, unlike Rule 184.

s: Under which Rules are 'Special Mentions' made in the Rajya Sabha?
x: Special Mentions in the Rajya Sabha come under Rules 180A–E; Rule 377 is the Lok Sabha equivalent for other matters.

s: Under which Rule is the no-confidence motion moved in the Lok Sabha?
x: Rule 198 governs the no-confidence motion; Rule 222 is the privilege motion and Rule 184 a discussion with vote.

s: A matter under Rule 377 is raised after written notice to the Secretary-General and with whose consent?
x: Rule 377 matters need written notice to the Secretary-General and the Speaker's consent.

s: Since 2015, what is the maximum number of matters that can be raised daily under Rule 377?
x: Up to 30 matters a day can be raised under Rule 377 since 2015; Zero Hour lasts at most one hour.

s: What is a motion raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts called?
x: A privilege motion targets a Minister who withheld or distorted facts; a censure motion disapproves of specific policies.

s: Which of the following statements about a Privilege Motion is incorrect?
o: It automatically forces the Government to resign.
It may be raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts.
It requires the consent of the Presiding Officer.
It is admissible in either House of Parliament.
x: Option A is incorrect: a privilege motion does not make the government resign. It is raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts, needs the presiding officer's consent and goes to the Committee of Privileges.

s: In which House can a privilege motion against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts be moved?
x: A privilege motion can be moved in either House with the presiding officer's consent and does not force resignation.

s: From what does the office of Whip in the Indian parliamentary system primarily derive its authority?
o: The Rules of Procedure of Parliament
A specific provision of the Constitution
x: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any parliamentary statute. It is based on conventions of parliamentary government.

s: On which days are Private Members' Resolutions in Parliament generally taken up?
o: The last sitting day of every month
x: Private Members’ Resolutions are taken up on alternate Fridays during the afternoon.

s: What is a resolution moved under a constitutional or statutory provision called?
x: Such a resolution is a statutory resolution; a Government resolution is one moved by a minister, e.g. to approve a treaty.

s: For how long is a resolution on the same subject barred after a resolution has been moved in Parliament?
x: A resolution on the same subject is barred for one year; a resolution is always a substantive motion, must be put to vote, and cannot be withdrawn without the House's leave.

s: Which Union Minister maintains close contact with the Chief Whips of political parties in both Houses of Parliament?
o: Minister of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
x: The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs keeps close contact with the Chief Whips of parties in both Houses.

s: Under which Schedule can defiance of a party Whip attract disqualification?
x: The Whip enforces attendance and voting on party lines, and defiance can attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Two-line Whip – Direction to attend the House
One-line Whip – Direction to attend the House
x: A two-line Whip directs members to attend; a one-line Whip is informative and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.

s: With what can the mover withdraw a resolution moved in Parliament?
o: Consent of the Business Advisory Committee
x: A resolution is a substantive motion that must be put to vote; the mover cannot withdraw it without leave of the House.

s: What does a three-line whip direct members to do?
o: Vote strictly as the party directs
x: A one-line whip informs, a two-line whip directs attendance and a three-line whip is a strict voting direction.

s: To which committee is a privilege motion referred?
x: A privilege motion goes to the Committee of Privileges.

s: Under Article 111, what may the President do when a Money Bill is presented to him?
o: Refer it to a joint sitting
x: The President may assent to or withhold assent from a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration.

s: Under Article 110(2), a Bill is NOT a Money Bill merely because it deals with which of the following?
x: A Bill only about fines or penalties is not a Money Bill; taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund are Money Bill matters.

s: Which one of the following is included within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1) of the Constitution?
o: Fees for licences issued by local authorities
Taxes imposed by a municipality for local purposes
Imposition of fines by a criminal court
Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax. Fines, licence fees and local taxes are not, by themselves, matters of a Money Bill.

s: Within how many days must the Rajya Sabha return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha?
x: The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days, with or without recommendations; otherwise it is deemed passed by both Houses.

s: Which case upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill, while the Money-Bill issue was subsequently referred to a larger bench in another case?
x: The Aadhaar Act was upheld as a Money Bill in K.S. Puttaswamy (2018). The Money-Bill question was later referred to a seven-judge bench in Rojer Mathew (2019).

s: Under Article 110(3), who decides finally whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
x: The Speaker's decision is final, and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.

s: In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Money Bill question was referred to a larger bench of how many judges?
x: Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the Money Bill question to a larger 7-judge bench.

s: Under Article 110(2), a Bill is NOT a Money Bill merely because it provides for taxes imposed by whom?
x: Taxes by local bodies for local purposes, fines and licence fees do not make a Bill a Money Bill.

s: The Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill is endorsed when the Bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha and to whom?
x: The certificate is endorsed when the Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha (Art. 109) and to the President (Art. 111).

s: What happens if the Rajya Sabha does not return the Appropriation Bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days?
o: It is deemed to have been passed by both Houses
It goes back to the President
x: The Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill. If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.

s: In which House, by whom and on whose recommendation can a Money Bill be introduced?
o: In either House by any member with the Speaker's consent
In the Rajya Sabha by a minister on the President's recommendation
In the Lok Sabha by a private member with the Rajya Sabha's approval
In the Lok Sabha by a minister on the President's recommendation
x: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, only by a minister, and only on the President's recommendation.

s: What can the Rajya Sabha do with the Annual Financial Statement?
o: Vote on the Demands for Grants
Discuss it but not vote on the Demands for Grants
x: The Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement, but voting on Demands for Grants (Art. 113) is only in the Lok Sabha.

s: Demands for Grants are provided for under which Article?
x: Article 113 deals with Demands for Grants; 112 is the Annual Financial Statement, 114 the Appropriation Bill and 116 the vote on account.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Constitution Amendment Bills come under Article 368; ordinary Bills under Articles 107–108, Money Bills under 109–110 and Financial Bills (I) under 117(1).

s: Which Article of the Constitution provides that the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses?
x: Article 118(4) says the Speaker presides over a joint sitting; Article 108 only provides for summoning it.

s: Which one of the following sets contains only the categories of Bills excluded from a joint sitting?
o: Private Members' Bills and Government Bills
Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills
x: Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills cannot be referred to a joint sitting. Financial Bills of types I and II can go to a joint sitting.

s: In counting the six-month period for a joint sitting under Article 108, adjournments of more than how many consecutive days are excluded?
x: Periods of prorogation and adjournment over four consecutive days are excluded; rejection or final disagreement on amendments are the other grounds.

s: At a joint sitting of the two Houses under Article 108, if both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are absent, who presides?
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President)
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
The senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
x: The order is: Speaker, then Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and failing all three, a member chosen by those present. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (the Vice-President) does not preside over a joint sitting, the President only summons it, and there is no rule for the senior-most Lok Sabha member.

s: What happens to the Bill if the President does not summon a joint sitting after a deadlock under Article 108?
o: Automatically becomes law after six months
Must be referred to the Supreme Court
Is deemed passed by both Houses
x: If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill comes to an end; it does not become law automatically.

s: How is a decision taken at a joint sitting of the two Houses?
o: A unanimous vote of the presiding officers of both Houses
A simple majority of members present and voting in both Houses together
A special majority of the total membership of both Houses
A two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each House separately
x: The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.

s: On which Bill was the joint sitting of Parliament held in 2002?
x: Joint sittings were held in 1961 (Dowry Prohibition), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal) and 2002 (Prevention of Terrorism).

s: What is the quorum of a joint sitting of the two Houses of Parliament?
x: The quorum of a joint sitting is one-tenth of the total membership of both Houses.

s: On which Bill was the first joint sitting of Parliament held in 1961?
x: Only three joint sittings have been held: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal) and 2002 (POTA).

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a joint sitting under Article 108?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides
Financial Bills I and II can be referred to it
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides in the Speaker's absence
Decisions are taken by a majority of members present and voting
x: The Vice-President / Rajya Sabha Chairman does not preside over a joint sitting; after the Speaker and Deputy Speaker comes the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman.

s: Under Article 108, what does the President do to start the process of a joint sitting of the two Houses?
o: He issues a direction to the Speaker to hold a joint sitting
He seeks the consent of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
He notifies to the Houses his intention to summon them to a joint sitting
He refers the Bill to the Supreme Court for advice
x: Article 108 uses the words 'notifies his intention' to summon a joint sitting. After this, neither House proceeds further with the Bill.

s: On which Bill was the joint sitting of Parliament held in 1978?
x: The three joint sittings were held in 1961 (Dowry Prohibition), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal) and 2002 (Prevention of Terrorism).

s: Which of the following is NOT a ground for summoning a joint sitting under Article 108?
o: The other House rejects the Bill
The two Houses finally disagree on amendments to the Bill
More than six months pass without the other House passing the Bill
The other House does not return the Bill within 14 days
x: The three grounds are rejection, final disagreement on amendments, and six months' delay; the 14-day limit applies only to Money Bills, which never go to a joint sitting.

s: Can a joint sitting be summoned for a Bill that has lapsed on dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: No, a joint sitting cannot be held for a lapsed Bill
Yes, within six months of dissolution
Yes, if the Rajya Sabha so requests
x: A joint sitting cannot be summoned for a Bill that has already lapsed; dissolution can end the Bill before the deadlock procedure operates.

s: The creation of a new All-India Service under Article 312 begins with a resolution of which body?
x: Creation of a new All-India Service starts with a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312.

s: A Government Bill in Parliament ordinarily requires what period of notice before introduction, whereas a Private Member's Bill requires what period?
x: A Government Bill requires seven days' notice, while a Private Member's Bill requires one month's notice before introduction.

s: Who normally drafts a Government Bill?
o: Concerned department in association with the Law Ministry
x: A Government Bill is drafted by the concerned department with the Law Ministry; a Private Member's Bill is drafted by the member.

s: In which year was the last Private Member's Bill enacted into law?
x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in 1970.

s: In the Rajya Sabha, which committee allots time for Private Members' Bills?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
x: The Rajya Sabha has no Committee on Private Members' Bills; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.

s: In the Lok Sabha, which committee allots time for Private Members' Bills?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
x: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions allots the time; defeat of such a Bill has no bearing on the government.

s: How many Private Members' Bills have become law so far?
x: Only 14 Private Members' Bills have become law, the last in 1970.

s: Who can introduce a Private Member's Bill?
o: Any MP who is not a minister
Only the Leader of the Opposition
x: Any MP who is not a minister may introduce a Private Member's Bill; Government Bills are introduced by ministers.

s: What does the defeat of a Government Bill in the House signal?
o: Automatic dissolution of the Lok Sabha
Reference of the Bill to a joint sitting
Loss of confidence in the government
x: Defeat of a Government Bill signals loss of confidence; defeat of a Private Member's Bill has no bearing on the government.

s: Which of the following is correct about Government Bills and Private Members' Bills?
o: A Private Member's Bill is passed in a single reading
A Government Bill needs one month's notice for introduction
A Private Member's Bill is drafted by the Law Ministry
Both pass through the same readings and stages in each House
x: Government and Private Members' Bills follow the same general procedure and stages. A Government Bill needs 7 days' notice and is drafted by the department with the Law Ministry.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Private Member's Bill needs one month's notice before introduction.
2. The defeat of a Private Member's Bill means loss of confidence in the government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: A Private Member's Bill needs one month's notice. Its defeat has no bearing on the government; only the defeat of a Government Bill signals loss of confidence.

s: Which committee of the Lok Sabha examines Private Members' Bills seeking to amend the Constitution before they are introduced?
o: Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions
x: In the Lok Sabha, the Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions classifies such Bills, allots time and examines private members' constitutional amendment Bills before introduction.

s: At which stage of a Bill does clause-by-clause consideration take place?
x: The Second Reading covers general discussion, committee stage and clause-by-clause voting; the Third Reading concerns the Bill as a whole.

s: After an ordinary Bill is passed by one House, what may the other House do?
o: Return it only to the President
Pass it, amend it, reject it, or keep it pending for six months
Certify it as a Money Bill
x: The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.

s: Which Amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill?
x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made it obligatory for the President to assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

s:
Consider the following statements about the second House on an ordinary Bill:
1. It may keep the Bill pending for six months, leading to a deadlock.
2. It must return the Bill within 14 days.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: For an ordinary Bill the second House has no time limit; the 14-day limit applies to the Rajya Sabha on a Money Bill.

s: A Bill is published in the Gazette at which stage of its passage?
x: At the first reading the Bill is introduced, its title and objectives are read and it is published in the Gazette.

s: If a Bill returned by the President is passed again by Parliament, the President must assent. What is this power called?
x: Returning a Bill once is a suspensive veto; if re-passed, with or without amendment, the President must assent.

s: Why is a 'pocket veto' possible for the President of India?
o: The President can return a Bill any number of times
The Constitution fixes no time limit for the President to decide on a Bill
The President can reject a Money Bill after the Rajya Sabha passes it
The President can refer every Bill to a joint sitting
x: Article 111 sets no time limit for the President's decision, so the President can keep a Bill pending. India has no qualified veto.

s: Which of the following Bills can the President NOT return to Parliament for reconsideration?
x: A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration, whereas Financial Bills-I and II can be.

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
x: Article 113 deals with Demands for Grants; the Appropriation Bill is under Article 114.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Money Bill — Joint sitting not permitted
x: A Financial Bill-I does not require the Speaker's certificate. A Money Bill requires that certificate; joint sitting is permitted for Financial Bills-I and II but not for a Money Bill.

s: In which House can a Financial Bill-I under Article 117(1) be introduced?
x: It is introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject it.

s: Which Bill gives effect to the tax proposals of the Budget?
x: The Finance Bill gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals; every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.

s: A Financial Bill-II under Article 117(3) needs the President's recommendation at which stage?
x: A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House and needs the President's recommendation only at the consideration stage.

s: A proposed amendment to a Financial Bill-I seeks to abolish an existing tax. Is the President's recommendation required for such an amendment?
o: No, because Financial Bills-I never require recommendation
Yes, because every amendment to a tax requires recommendation
No, an amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require such recommendation
Yes, but only when the Bill is pending in the Rajya Sabha
x: An amendment reducing or abolishing a tax does not require the President's recommendation. An amendment increasing a tax requires such recommendation.

s: Which of the following Bills may be introduced by a private member?
x: Only a Financial Bill-II may be introduced by a minister or a private member; Money Bills (including the Appropriation Bill) and FB-I by a minister only.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Financial Bill-I is under Article 117(1); the Money Bill is defined in Article 110, FB-II is Article 117(3) and the joint sitting is Article 108.

s: Which of the following is NOT required for a Financial Bill-I?
o: Introduction only in the Lok Sabha
x: A Financial Bill-I needs no Speaker's certificate; that is required only for a Money Bill.

s: Which Bill, giving effect to the tax proposals of the Budget, is usually certified by the Speaker as a Money Bill?
x: The Finance Bill puts the Budget's tax proposals into effect and is usually certified as a Money Bill.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 117(3) — Financial Bill-II at the consideration stage
Article 3 — Formation of new States or alteration of their areas, boundaries or names
Article 274 — Bills relating exclusively to expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India
x: Article 274 concerns Bills affecting taxation in which States are interested. Bills involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India require recommendation under Article 117(3).

s: What does a State Bill imposing restrictions on inter-state trade need before its introduction in the State Legislature?
x: A State Bill restricting inter-state trade needs the President's previous sanction before introduction.

s: Under which Article does a Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested need the President's prior recommendation?
x: Article 274 requires the President's prior recommendation for Bills on taxation in which States are interested.

s: On dissolution of the Lok Sabha, which of the following Bills lapses?
o: A Bill returned by the President for reconsideration
A Bill passed by both Houses and awaiting the President's assent
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha has not passed
A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha
x: A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses; the other three survive dissolution.

s: A joint sitting of Parliament has already been notified before the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. What is the position of the bill concerned?
o: It does not lapse merely because of dissolution
It must be returned to the Rajya Sabha for fresh introduction
It becomes a Money Bill automatically
x: A bill for which a joint sitting has been notified before dissolution does not lapse merely on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

s: On dissolution of the Lok Sabha, what happens to a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha has never passed?
o: goes automatically to a joint sitting
x: Such a Bill survives dissolution, while Bills pending in the Lok Sabha or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapse; prorogation ends no Bill.

s: Which of the following causes all pending business before the Lok Sabha to lapse?
x: Only dissolution makes all pending Lok Sabha business lapse; adjournment or adjournment sine die does not make Bills lapse.

s: On prorogation of a House, which of the following lapses?
o: Pending notices, except notices for introducing Bills
All pending business of the House
Bills passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha
x: Prorogation does not end Bills; only pending notices lapse, except notices for introducing Bills.

s: Which of the following Bills does NOT lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha
A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha
A Bill passed by both Houses and pending the President's assent
A Bill passed by the Rajya Sabha and pending in the Lok Sabha
x: A Bill passed by both Houses and pending assent survives dissolution; Bills pending in or passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapse.

s: What happens to Bills pending before a House of Parliament when the House is adjourned sine die?
o: They do not lapse and are taken up in the next session
They are sent to a joint sitting
They are deemed to have been passed
x: Adjournment sine die ends a sitting without fixing a day to meet again; pending Bills do not lapse and continue in the next session.

s: Which new Article is proposed by the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 on simultaneous elections?
x: The Bill proposes Article 82A; it remained before the Joint Parliamentary Committee and has not been enacted.

s: By what majority must a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368 be passed in each House?
o: A simple majority of members present and voting
Two-thirds of the total membership only
Three-fourths of members present and voting
A majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting
x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill needs a special majority in each House separately: majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.

s: What happens if the two Houses disagree on a Constitutional Amendment Bill?
o: No joint sitting can be held
The President summons a joint sitting
The Bill is referred to the Supreme Court
x: There is no joint sitting for a Constitutional Amendment Bill; it must pass each House separately.

s:
Consider the following statements about a Constitutional Amendment Bill:
1. It needs the President's prior recommendation for introduction.
2. It can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill can start in either House, by a minister or private member, and needs no prior recommendation of the President.

s: A Constitutional Amendment Bill that changes the federal provisions must be ratified by how many State Legislatures?
x: Under Article 368, an amendment of federal provisions also needs ratification by the legislatures of half of the States.

s:
Consider the following statements about a Constitutional Amendment Bill under Article 368:
1. It must be passed in each House separately by a special majority.
2. If it affects federal provisions, it must be ratified by half of the States.
3. A deadlock between the two Houses on it can be settled at a joint sitting.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: It needs a special majority in each House and ratification by half the States for federal provisions; there is no joint sitting for such a Bill.

s: What can the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council do in relation to a Money Bill?
o: refer it to a joint sitting within fourteen days
amend it finally within fourteen days
x: The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill within fourteen days. It cannot reject or amend the Bill finally.

s: Which of the following is NOT an option available to the Governor under Article 200?
o: Returning a Money Bill for reconsideration
Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President
Assenting to a Bill passed by the State Legislature
x: The Governor cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about timelines for assent to State Bills?
o: The April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor judgment laid down fixed timelines for Governors.
The November 2025 opinion upheld the deemed assent granted in the Tamil Nadu case.
In November 2025, a five-judge Bench advised on a Presidential Reference that courts cannot fix such timelines.
x: The November 2025 advisory opinion held that courts cannot fix timelines or declare deemed assent, so it did not uphold the Tamil Nadu deemed assent.

s: Under Article 200, for whose consideration may the Governor reserve a State Bill?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
x: The Governor may assent, withhold, return a non-Money Bill or reserve it for the President under Article 201.

s: Under which Article was the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, renaming the State 'Keralam', brought?
x: Alteration of a State's name is under Article 3; the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 was passed by the Rajya Sabha.

s: On which date did the Andhra State Bill, introduced in Parliament on 10 August 1953, receive assent?
x: The Andhra State Bill was introduced on 10 August 1953 and received assent on 14 September 1953.

s: What did the Supreme Court hold about courts in its November 2025 advisory opinion on a Presidential Reference?
o: Cannot fix timelines for assent or declare deemed assent
Can fix timelines for assent to State Bills
Can declare deemed assent to State Bills
Can give assent on behalf of the Governor
x: The five-judge Bench held that courts cannot fix timelines or declare deemed assent, unlike the April 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor judgment.

s: In the Monsoon Session of 2026, which Bill was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee?
x: The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was referred to a JPC in the Monsoon Session 2026, after a push by the united opposition.

s: By what name does the Constitution refer to the Union Budget?
x: Article 112 uses 'Annual Financial Statement'; the word 'Budget' does not occur in the Constitution.

s: In which month is the Budget Circular, which begins the Budget process, generally issued?
x: The Budget Circular is generally issued in September, and printing of Budget documents is marked by the Halwa ceremony.

s: The Union Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of which Department?
o: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
x: The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division in the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.

s: On which date did R.K. Shanmukham Chetty present the first Union Budget of independent India?
x: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on 26 November 1947.

s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the Appropriation Bill?
x: Article 114 covers the Appropriation Bill; Article 112 is the Annual Financial Statement and Article 116 the vote on account.

s: Which Article provides for the vote on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants?
x: Article 116 covers these; 112 is the Annual Financial Statement, 113 the estimates procedure and 115 supplementary, additional or excess grants.

s: In which two parts is the Union Budget presented?
x: The Budget covers the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account and is presented in Revenue and Capital parts.

s: By whose order is the Annual Financial Statement laid before both Houses of Parliament?
x: The President causes the AFS to be laid before both Houses; it is presented in the Lok Sabha by the Finance Minister.

s: What does the Halwa ceremony in North Block mark?
o: Start of printing of Budget documents
x: The Halwa ceremony marks the start of printing of Budget documents.

s: What does the French word 'bougette', from which 'Budget' comes, mean?
x: 'Bougette' is French for little bag; the Constitution itself does not use the word 'Budget'.

s: Who presented the Union Budget for 2023-24 in the Lok Sabha?
x: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman presented the Union Budget 2023-24 in the Lok Sabha.

s: Who presented the Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27 on 14 February 2026?
x: Finance Minister Payyavula Keshav presented the main Budget; K. Atchannaidu presented the separate agriculture budget.

s: On which date was the Union Budget for 2026-27 presented?
x: The Union Budget 2026-27 was presented on 1 February 2026. The date 14 February 2026 relates to the presentation of the Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27.

s: What is the proposed size of the Economic Stabilisation Fund in the Union Budget 2026-27?
x: The proposed Economic Stabilisation Fund is Rs 1 lakh crore; Rs 30,000 crore is the corpus of the Contingency Fund of India.

s: In which year was the Railway Budget merged with the Union Budget?
x: The Railway Budget, separate since 1924, was merged with the Union Budget in 2017.

s: To which year do the first Outcome Budget and the first Gender Budget Statement relate?
x: Both the first Outcome Budget and the first Gender Budget Statement were in 2005-06.

s: Who presented the first combined Railway and General Budget on 1 February 2017?
